title: The main table
objectives: Say what each cell of the main table measures.

screens.title: The layout
screens.prose: Jegadeesh and Titman (1993), "Returns to Buying Winners and Selling Losers" (JT), print their main table in this layout. For each J there are three rows: losers (Sell), winners (Buy) and the spread (Buy − Sell). Columns are K. These numbers are from our seeded panel.

state.caption: Seeded stand-in in the paper's layout, % a month. Legs and spread are rounded separately.

screens.question: Tap the cell that measures the 6-month/6-month strategy.

hints.text: The strategy buys winners and sells losers. Which row is that?
Look in the J = 6 rows, in the column headed 6.
The Buy − Sell row for J = 6, in the K = 6 column.

feedback.correct: Correct. 0.96% a month for 6/6 on our panel.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the Buy − Sell row for J = 6, then the K = 6 column.

byKey.r1c3: That is the Buy row: the winners alone. The strategy is Buy minus Sell.
byKey.r0c3: That is the Sell row: the losers' return. The strategy subtracts it.
byKey.r2c2: That column is K = 3. The 6/6 strategy holds for six months.
byKey.r5c3: That row is J = 12. The 6/6 strategy ranks on six months.

explain.text: Each cell is the average monthly return of one portfolio over the sample. The Buy − Sell row is the strategy: 0.96% a month on our panel for 6/6. The paper reports about 0.95% for the same cell.

screens.title: Across the grid
screens.prose: Here is only the Buy − Sell row for each J, the sixteen strategies the paper studies. Look along each row and down each column.

state.caption: Our seeded panel, Buy − Sell in % a month, no skip. A stand-in for the paper's table.

screens.question: Tap the largest cell and the smallest cell.

hints.text: Scan for the biggest and smallest numbers.
Both lie in the K = 3 column.
12/3 at 1.31 is the largest and 3/3 at 0.51 the smallest.

feedback.correct: Correct. 12/3 is the largest and 3/3 the smallest.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare all sixteen numbers.

byKey.r3c4: 12/12 is small at 0.66, but 3/3 is smaller at 0.51.
byKey.r1c1: 6/3 is 0.91. The K = 3 column holds both ends, at J = 3 and J = 12.
byKey.r2c0: That cell is a row label. Tap a number.

explain.text: The spread rises as J grows and falls as K grows beyond about 6. The paper reports its most profitable cell as 12/3, about 1.31% a month, and ours is 1.31% too. That match is by design: the generator was tuned to the paper.

screens.title: The t statistic
screens.prose: Under each mean the paper prints a **t statistic**: the mean over its standard error. The standard error is the sd over $\sqrt{n}$. Our 6/6 series has mean 0.96%, sd 5.98% and 289 months.
screens.question: What is the 6/6 t statistic, to 2 decimal places?

hints.text: First find the standard error.
$\sqrt{289} = 17$, so the standard error is 5.98% / 17.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the mean by sd / √n.

byKey.sd: You divided by the sd itself. Divide the sd by √289 = 17 first.
byKey.root: You divided by √n instead of multiplying the sd ratio by it. The t is mean / (sd / √n).

explain.text: The standard error is 5.98% / 17 = 0.352%, so t = 0.96 / 0.352 = 2.73, or 2.74 from unrounded inputs. That is past 1.96 and 2.58. The paper reports t statistics of about 3 to 4.

screens.title: High mean, low t
screens.prose: Two cells from our grid. 12/12 has mean 0.66% a month with t 1.77. 3/12 has mean 0.63% a month with t 2.98.
screens.question: Which cell is the stronger evidence of a spread above zero?

options.why: You compared the means. 12/12 is noisier, so its t is only 1.77, below 1.96.

options.text: Neither: the means are almost equal
options.why: Equal means can carry very different evidence. The t accounts for the noise.

hints.text: Which number measures evidence, the mean or the t?
Compare each t with 1.96.
3/12 is past 2.58; 12/12 is short of 1.96.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Evidence is the mean measured against its noise.

explain.text: The two means differ by 0.03%, but the t statistics differ a lot. 12/12's spread swings more, so its standard error is larger and its t falls short of 1.96. A cell is read as mean and t together.

screens.title: Monthly to yearly
screens.prose: The paper reports about 0.95% a month for 6/6, and its abstract gives 12.01% a year. Returns compound: each month earns on the gains before it.
screens.question: What is 0.95% a month compounded over 12 months, in % a year?

hints.text: Grow £1 by 0.95% twelve times.
£1 × 1.0095¹² is the value after a year.

byKey.simple: You multiplied by 12. Returns compound, so each month also earns on the last month's gain.

explain.text: $(1.0095)^{12} - 1 = 0.1201$, the abstract's 12.01%. Multiplying by 12 gives 11.40%, which misses the compounding. So the abstract and the table say the same thing in two units.

screens.title: The Sell row
screens.prose: Our 6/6 strategy's ten deciles, averaged over the sample. The losers (D1, the Sell row) earn 1.04% a month and the winners (D10, Buy) 2.01%. A colleague says: "The losers make money, so selling them loses money."

state.caption: Seeded panel, J = 6, K = 6: mean monthly return of each decile's composite

screens.question: What does the 6/6 strategy earn a month?

options.why: You added the two legs. The losers are sold, so their return is subtracted.
You read the Sell row alone. Both legs earn positive returns here; the strategy earns the gap between them.
That is the long leg alone. The short leg costs the losers' 1.04%.

hints.text: You are long the winners and short the losers.
The short side loses what the losers gain.
2.01 − 1.04, about 0.96 after rounding.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Long winners, short losers: subtract.

byKey.sell-loss: You read the Sell row as the strategy's loss. In JT's tables both legs can earn positive returns; what matters is the spread.

explain.text: The short losers cost 1.04% and the winners earn 2.01%, so the strategy earns the gap. Rounded legs give 0.97; the unrounded spread is 0.96. A positive Sell row only means losers rose less than winners.

screens.title: Reading any cell
screens.prose: A cell reports a mean and a t statistic. An annual figure follows by compounding. $$\bar x = \tfrac{1}{n}\textstyle\sum_t x_t,\quad t = \dfrac{\bar x}{s / \sqrt{n}},\quad r_{\text{year}} = (1 + \bar x)^{12} - 1$$ Here $x_t$ is the Buy − Sell return in month $t$ and $s$ its sd.
screens.question: A cell has mean 0.80% and standard error 0.40%. What is its t?

options.why: You divided the standard error by the mean. The t is mean over standard error.
You multiplied. The t divides the mean by its standard error.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the mean by its standard error.

explain.text: 0.80 / 0.40 = 2.0, just past 1.96. The standard error already includes the √n. So a cell's t reads directly from its mean and standard error.

screens.title: The two numbers in code
screens.prose: Write the two calculations a cell needs, in plain Python with no NumPy. The sample sd divides by $n - 1$.

state.caption: Our seeded panel, Buy − Sell in % a month, no skip. A stand-in for the paper's table.

hints.text: Compounding is a power, not a product with 12.
The sample variance divides the squared deviations by n − 1.
`var = sum((v - mean) ** 2 for v in x) / (n - 1)` and `return mean / (math.sqrt(var) / math.sqrt(n))`.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Check the power in `annualise` and the n − 1 in `t_stat`.

explain.text: `(1 + m) ** 12 - 1` compounds twelve months. The t divides the mean by the sd with n − 1 over √n. With ddof 0, `t_stat([1, 3])` would give 2.83 instead of 2.0.

screens.title: After costs
screens.prose: A portfolio manager reads a research summary: "1% a month, t 3". Her first question is what it earns after trading costs. The 6/6 design trades 0.577 of its book each month, counting buys and sells.
screens.question: What is the spread after costs, in % a month?

hints.text: The cost is charged on every £1 traded.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply what is traded by the cost per £1, then subtract.

byKey.one-side: You charged only half the trading. The 0.577 already counts both sides; charge 25 bp on all of it.
byKey.flat: You subtracted 25 bp once. The cost is per £1 traded, and the book trades 0.577 a month.

explain.text: Costs are 0.577 × 0.25% = 0.144% a month, so 1.00% becomes about 0.86%. Our panel's 6/6 cell falls from 0.96% to 0.82% the same way. Level 2 builds the turnover itself.

ideas: Each cell is the average monthly Buy − Sell return of one J/K strategy over the sample.
Its t statistic is the mean over its standard error, $s/\sqrt{n}$.

formula.name: The t statistic
formula.note: Mean over standard error; past 1.96 is significant at 5%.

summary.trap: Adding the Buy and Sell rows, or reading a positive Sell row as a loss. The strategy earns Buy minus Sell.

quiz.prose: A strategy earns 0.5% a month on average.
quiz.question: What is that compounded over a year, in %?

byKey.simple: You multiplied by 12. Compounding adds the return on earlier gains.

explain.text: $(1.005)^{12} - 1 = 0.0617$. The 0.17% above 6% is interest on interest.

quiz.prose: In a paper's table, one J/K cell shows Sell 1.20% and Buy 1.70% a month.
quiz.question: What does the strategy earn, in % a month?

feedback.generic: Not quite. The strategy is long Buy and short Sell.

byKey.add: You added the rows. The Sell portfolio is sold, so subtract it.
byKey.sell: You took the Sell row as the result. The strategy earns Buy minus Sell.

explain.text: Long winners at 1.70% and short losers at 1.20% earn the 0.50% gap. Both legs earn positive returns; the spread is the strategy.

quiz.prose: A spread has mean 0.8% a month, sd 5% and 100 months of data.
quiz.question: What is its t statistic?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the mean by sd / √n.

byKey.sd: You divided by the sd. Divide it by √100 = 10 first.

explain.text: The standard error is 5% / 10 = 0.5%, so t = 0.8 / 0.5 = 1.6. That is short of 1.96.

quiz.prose: Our 12/12 cell has mean 0.66% a month and t 1.77.
quiz.question: Which reading is right?

options.text: The mean is positive, but noise alone could produce a t that large

options.why: A t below 1.96 does not show the mean is zero. It shows the data cannot rule zero out.

options.text: It is strong evidence, because 0.66% a month is large
options.why: You judged by the mean alone. The t says the noise is too large for that.

feedback.correct: Correct. Not significant at 5%, not proven zero.
feedback.generic: Not quite. A t below 1.96 is weak evidence, not evidence of zero.

explain.text: A t of 1.77 is short of the 1.96 cut-off. The data are consistent with a spread of zero and with one of 0.66%. More months or less noise would decide it.
